https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: A child and three firefighters were taken to hospital following the wildfire in Stourbridge as England once again joined a long – and growing – list of countries battling active fires during this year’s extraordinarily extremely hot summer. With the hottest day of the year recorded in England on Thursday, the temperatures are expected to start to fall, but just slightly, on Friday, with low to mid 30s expected. Across the channel, France is also expecting another hot day after temperatures of up to 41C on Thursday. Over 500 people were evacuated from the southwestern Landes region. Over in Greece, hundreds of tourists were evacuated from the popular hotspot of Halkidiki, as firefighters continue to fight a large blaze amid gale-force winds. At least 19 people were also injured in a fire near the Croatian tourist town of Omiš, with two people requiring hospitalisation in the popular city of Split. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Automated EES kiosks at Madrid airport. The EU rejected calls to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. Photograph: Juan Medina/Reuters View image in fullscreen Automated EES kiosks at Madrid airport. The EU rejected calls to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. Photograph: Juan Medina/Reuters Travel & leisure ‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellers Britons report that EES digital entry and exit system has led to frustration, visa mix-ups and long queues Jane Clinton and Rosie Peters-McDonald Sun 23 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 15.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n top of fears about extreme heat and possible jet fuel shortages , Britons planning summer holidays in the EU this year had another thing to worry about – long queues and waiting times caused by the bloc’s new border checks. The EU digital entry and exit system (EES) , which requires non-EU citizens to register and be photographed and fingerprinted on arrival and departure from the Schengen zone, has been technically in full force since April after launching last autumn , but has been beset by teething problems. Despite reports of passengers facing three-hour delays and missed connections, Brussels rejected calls by airports and airlines to suspend the implementation of the scheme over the peak summer period. However, border police have been allowed to relax requirements if queues become unmanageable under an opt-out that expires next month. What are the new EU border checks and how will they affect your summer holiday? Read more Those who shared with the Guardian their experiences of the system since its introduction highlighted a range of problems and snags. ‘We checked in to Europe, but the EES says we haven’t checked out’ View image in fullscreen Martin in Silkeborg, Denmark, on a paddle steamer with his dog, Morris. Photograph: Martin/Guardian Community One of the main purposes of the system is to track whether non-EU citizens have spent more than their permitted 90 days in the bloc in a rolling 180-day period. However, Martin Farrall, a retired university professor, says his EES record failed to record his exit from the Schengen zone and he had to chase the authorities to update it. In May, the 67-year-old and his wife arrived by ferry at Hoek van Holland at the start of their camping trip in Denmark, both with a full residency allowance. Martin says the Dutch border police enrolled them into EES “But no entry stamp was made on our passports,” he adds. “On 30 June, 55 days after entry, we returned to the UK on the Dunkerque-Dover ferry. The French border police asked us where and when we entered Schengen, and we were handed back our passports without an exit stamp.” Once home, Martin checked his residency tally and found that instead of having 35 days left it was rapidly diminishing. View image in fullscreen Martin on a forest walk in Denmark with Morris. Photograph: Martin/Guardian Community “It appeared that EES had not been updated to show I’d left the Schengen area,” says Martin, who lives in Warwickshire. He was concerned that he would be registered as an “overstayer” at risk of refusal of entry in future. He reported the error to the Directorate General for Foreign Nationals in France on 13 July but says he has not received a response.. When Martin checked on his day allowance again on 7 August, the EES website said he had zero days left, but when he looked on 17 August it had updated. “The EES website now claims I have 34 days left to travel in the 180 window! When I checked my wife’s passport she apparently has 90 days left despite us both having the same travel to Schengen history. So God only knows what’s going on. “I wonder how many other people who were waved through because of the hold-ups may also be in the same position.” ‘The system obviously wasn’t ready – it’s pretty shambolic’ Nadia, from Greater Manchester, thinks the system is not “communicating with other member states”. She made two trips to Schengen areas this summer with very contrasting experiences. A trip to Tenerife in June was “quite straightforward”, but her experience in July at Frankfurt airport where she was picking up a connecting flight home, was much less so. View image in fullscreen Nadia says she was not sure which queue she should join at Frankfurt airport. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters “The queue there was ridiculously long, and there was very limited information,” she says. “People were wandering around trying to work out where they needed to go. “I’m very well travelled and pretty confident, but even I was slightly unsure and was thinking, is there some other queue I should be joining? There was no one nearby to check with without losing your place.” Eventually, her passport was checked. “He didn’t actually take fingerprints then,” says Nadia, who is a solicitor. “I think the queue was so long they decided to dispense with that. “It’s the efficiency of the system I question and the fact that individual member states’ systems do not talk to one another. They shouldn’t need to get information again if you have already gone through. “It’s pretty shambolic, and I think people missing their flights because of it is just not acceptable, especially when there’s no recourse; it’s not your fault.” Nadia is also unhappy about having to give her fingerprints repeatedly. “I’ve done it in a few countries now, but it’s something I feel very strongly opposed to,” she says. “This is not in keeping with the intention of the scheme, which suggests that once registered, you should not have to keep re-entering your biometric data. You also wonder where the information is going – who’s seeing it, who else has access to it?” ‘There should be clearer signage about exemptions’ Evie, originally from Manchester but studying in Munich, says her student visa has caused EES confusion. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “In Munich airport, there are TV screens which explain the function of EES as a system to register ‘visitors’. As I hold an extended-stay visa for the purpose of studying, I would not describe myself as a ‘visitor’ as I can stay in Germany for up to 12 months,” the 23-year-old says. She says that upon seeing she had a British passport, she was often directed toward the EES queue and had to explain her visa situation, after which she “was normally allowed to stand in the queue with everyone else”. Evie says this has happened “virtually every time” she has flown in and out of Germany – in December, January, February and April – and believes there should be better signposting to avoid mix-ups, especially given unreliable airport wifi makes accessing online information difficult. ‘You could see people getting anxious’ Kevin and his wife, Christine, travelled to Lanzarote in June but struggled to get the machine to register their details. “The arrivals hall was packed, but there were loads of machines,” the 75-year-old says. “Some were not working. I noticed people getting angry when their fingerprints would not enter. People started holding their fingers in different positions, and when that didn’t work, they would hit the glass harder.” View image in fullscreen Kevin and Christine on holiday in Lanzarote in June 2026. Photograph: Kevin/Guardian Community He says there was “not much assistance to be found” and when all attempts failed, people queued up to “have it done manually at the kiosk”. “You could see people getting anxious,” says Kevin, who lives with Christine, 73, in Merseyside. He says the machines eventually registered them both. The couple’s next trip is to Palma for a cruise, and they are bracing themselves for there to be issues. “We’ll be visiting different countries on the cruise,” Kevin says. “What happens then?” ‘The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me’ Martin, 68, a retired IT worker, said he and his wife struggled to operate the screen to register at Schiphol airport in the Netherlands. “The fingerprinting system didn’t work for me,” says Martin of their trip at the end of April. “My wife had similar issues with her 71-year-old hands. Older people with drier fingers have trouble with touch screens.” Eventually, Martin, who lives in Stockport, was sent to manual entry “where they forgot to stamp my passport”. “When exiting Dusseldorf, the Germans got a bit excited about that and asked how we got into Europe ,” he adds. “I just said the Dutch didn’t stamp our passports, and they accepted that. “The interface is poorly laid out and will confuse the less technical I have an IT background, and it feels like the system was not walked through enough times. It’s a mess. It also hasn’t been properly tested for older people.” View image in fullscreen Travellers have reported problems with operating the digital touchscreens and fingerprint scanners used by the EES system. Photograph: Hugh Williamson/Alamy ‘My wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look’ Ed Griffiths, 67, a retired IT specialist, says his wife has impaired vision and could not work the machine at Prague airport as they passed through last September as she was unable to read the instructions. “The photo/fingerprint machine failed for both of us, and we spent one hour 15 minutes standing in a slow queue of confused people waiting for staff to retry it, but my wife, being visually impaired, couldn’t find where to look, so they skipped the photo and she was waved through,” says Ed, who lives in Buckinghamshire. The delay meant their prebooked taxi nearly left without them. Then the couple were in Milan in March and Ed had to re-register despite already having done so in Prague. “The machine ignored my previous registration, my fingerprint was asked for and failed, I waited an hour in a queue for manual assistance retry,” he says. His wife, also 67, however, did manage registration and was waved through. More recently, in Vienna in May an officer supervised the booths for photos and fingerprints. Again, the system ignored his previous registration, but the couple got through in five minutes. “Twice we have been registered already, and it made no discernible difference,” Ed says. “We have not found assistance at machines, but at booths there has been some help.” Get in touch Contact us about this story The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. http://english.anhuinews.com/newscenter/.text: EU Should pursue "friendly competition" with China, not trade barriers: Slovak PM EU Should pursue 'friendly competition' with China, not trade barriers: Slovak PM Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly competition" with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. BRATISLAVA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly competition" with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Their discussions covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." On the EU's next long-term budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. The two leaders also discussed EU enlargement. Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, but said all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. â

https://www.ynetnews.com/article/byiqgrh.text: Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar inaugurated Israel’s first-ever embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday, completing in just three months a diplomatic push driven by Ljubljana’s dramatic change of course toward Jerusalem and Israel’s search for reliable allies inside the European Union. The embassy, in central Ljubljana, is the fifth Sa’ar has opened in the past year and a half and comes as Slovenia emerges as one of Israel’s closest partners in the EU. For now, however, the mission is operating from temporary premises. The permanent embassy is intended to move to another space on a higher floor of the same office building, but that property has not yet become available. Israeli officials said there was an urgent need to establish a diplomatic presence before then, prompting security authorities to approve the temporary arrangement. A senior diplomatic official said Sa’ar promised the Slovenians in June that Israel would open an embassy after the new government reversed a string of measures adopted by its predecessor. Those changes included lifting a ban on Israir flights landing in Ljubljana, reversing recognition of a Palestinian state, removing a Palestinian flag from the Slovenian Foreign Ministry building, ending an arms embargo on Israel, revoking the designation of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as persona non grata and declaring an intention to move Slovenia’s embassy in Israel to Jerusalem. Officials also described a broader transformation in Slovenia’s position inside the European Union, from one of the bloc’s most hostile governments toward Israel to one of its friendliest. That shift was demonstrated last month when Slovenia and Czechia vetoed an initiative by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas to secure a joint condemnation by all 27 member states of Israel’s E1 construction plan. ‘You can’t leave the Czechs alone’ According to the senior official, Slovenia’s importance grew after the political upheaval in Hungary and the fall of Viktor Orban, whose government had been strongly supportive of Jerusalem. The change, the official said, created an opening for Kallas to seek unanimous EU decisions targeting Israel, including potential sanctions. “Czechia would not have been able to withstand the pressure alone, so it needed another country to support it,” the official said. “That is why there was urgency in opening the embassy in Ljubljana. You can’t leave the Czechs alone.” Sa’ar instructed Foreign Ministry Director General Eden Bar Tal to establish the mission, which was completed within three months, a timetable officials described as unprecedented. Sa’ar later traveled to Ljubljana with a delegation of Israeli businesspeople as part of a broader effort to deepen economic and political ties. “Israel had to show Slovenia that it was serious,” the official said. “Israel cannot do without Slovenia, and we are going full speed ahead in advancing relations in every field. Sa’ar’s directive is to strengthen the relationship with maximum effort.” Security officials approved the temporary embassy ahead of the planned relocation in several months. A senior Foreign Ministry official said Israel would not pay rent on both premises simultaneously. Once the intended space becomes available, the mission will move there without any overlap. “That was the security authorities’ condition for opening the embassy,” the official said. Another senior ministry official rejected suggestions that Sa’ar insisted on opening the embassy before Israel’s election for political reasons. “Sa’ar has established six embassies over the past year and a half, including when elections were not on the horizon,” the official said. “That is his policy. It is his forte.”
